title: Combinational Circuits
summary: Adders, multiplexers, and decoders are the reusable building blocks every datapath is assembled from — each just a fixed composition of the gates from the last two topics.

slides.markdown:
A **combinational circuit** has no memory: its output is a **pure function of its current inputs**, nothing else. Feed it the same inputs twice, in any order, at any time, and you always get the same output — there's no internal state carrying information from one evaluation to the next.

This is the opposite of a **sequential circuit** (next topic), where the output also depends on history (stored state). Every circuit this card covers — adders, muxes, decoders — is purely combinational; add feedback and memory, and you cross into sequential territory.

slides.subTitle: Half adder
slides.markdown:
A **half adder** adds two single bits, producing a sum and a carry — built from exactly two gates:

![A half adder: XOR gate producing the sum bit, AND gate producing the carry bit](assets/half-adder.svg)

`Sum = A XOR B` (true when exactly one input is 1 — matches binary addition without carry). `Carry = A AND B` (true only when both inputs are 1, which is exactly when adding two bits produces a carry). It's called 'half' because it has no carry-**in** — it can't be chained directly for multi-bit addition on its own.

assets.alt: A half adder: XOR gate producing the sum bit, AND gate producing the carry bit

slides.subTitle: Full adder
slides.markdown:
A **full adder** fixes the half adder's limitation by accepting a **carry-in**, making it chainable:

![A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate combining their carries](assets/full-adder.svg)

It's built from **two half adders plus an OR gate**: the first half adder adds A and B; the second adds that sum to the carry-in; the OR gate combines both half adders' carry outputs into the final carry-out. This chainability is exactly what a ripple-carry adder exploits.

assets.alt: A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate combining their carries

slides.subTitle: Ripple-carry's latency problem
slides.markdown:
Chain n full adders together — each one's carry-out feeding the next one's carry-in — and you get an n-bit **ripple-carry adder** (seen in the previous group's overflow topic). Simple to build, but the carry has to physically **propagate through every stage** before the final sum is valid.

For a 64-bit ripple-carry adder, the worst case (a carry that must ripple through all 64 stages) makes the adder's delay grow **linearly with width** — doubling the register width roughly doubles the addition latency, which becomes the dominant bottleneck in a wide ALU.

slides.subTitle: The multiplexer
slides.markdown:
A **multiplexer (mux)** selects one of several input signals to route to its output, based on a **select line** (or lines). A 2-to-1 mux picks input A or input B based on one select bit; an n-to-1 mux needs `log2(n)` select bits.

Beyond simple routing, a mux is a **universal function generator**: wiring the right constants and inputs into a mux's data inputs can implement *any* boolean function of the select lines — this is exactly why datapaths are full of muxes at every decision point (which ALU operand, which write-back source, which next-PC value).

slides.subTitle: Decoders and encoders
slides.markdown:
A **decoder** converts an n-bit address into one active output line out of `2^n` — exactly one output goes high, identifying which address was given. This is how a register file selects which single register to write, or how memory selects which row to activate.

An **encoder** does the reverse: given exactly one active input line out of `2^n`, it outputs the n-bit index of that line. Together they're the address<->one-hot conversion used constantly wherever hardware must select 'exactly one of many' resources.

slides.subTitle: Ripple-carry vs carry-lookahead
slides.markdown:
**Carry-lookahead adders** compute each stage's carry directly from the original inputs (via extra 'generate'/'propagate' logic) instead of waiting for it to ripple through every prior stage:

| | Ripple-carry | Carry-lookahead |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | Grows linearly with width | Grows much more slowly (roughly logarithmically with extra gating) |
| Gate cost | Minimal — just chained full adders | More gates (the lookahead logic itself) |
| Used when | Width is small, or area matters more than speed | Wide, performance-critical ALUs (most real CPUs) |

The trade is exactly the gate-delay-vs-area lesson from the last topic: carry-lookahead spends more silicon to buy a shorter critical path — real CPUs make this trade because addition latency directly caps clock speed.

slides.subTitle: A mux-based function selector

slides.sectionTitle: Decoders and encoders: the inverse pair
slides.markdown:
A **decoder** takes an N-bit binary code and activates exactly one of 2^N output lines — a 3-to-8 decoder takes input `101` and drives output line 5 high, all others low. This is the circuit behind every memory address decode (picking one row out of a RAM array) and every instruction opcode dispatch (picking one control-signal set out of an opcode field).

An **encoder** does the reverse: given one active input line out of 2^N, it outputs the N-bit binary code identifying which one. Real encoders are usually **priority encoders** — if multiple inputs are active at once (which a pure decoder's output never produces, but external inputs like interrupt lines routinely do), the encoder outputs the code for the highest-priority one and ignores the rest, rather than producing garbage.

You'll see this exact pair again in a CPU's interrupt controller: a priority encoder picks which of several pending interrupt lines to service first, and a decoder later turns that chosen code back into a single control signal that fetches the right handler.
